title: Palindromes
full_review:
A young girl's misguided search for love takes her on a bleak odyssey across the moral landscape of America in the intriguing but highly disturbing "Palindromes" (Wellspring).

In his ironically titled 1998 movie, "Happiness," director Todd Solondz used acerbic humor to plumb the depths of emotional dysfunction and sexual pathology -- including pedophilia -- in contemporary suburbia. In his latest offering, he plies a similar strain of shock-effect satire to probe the subject of abortion.

A "palindrome" is a word or phrase that read the same backward as forward, like the name of its 13-year-old protagonist, Aviva. In an unconventional and, at times distracting, casting move, the part is played by seven different actors of varying ages, races and genders, including four young girls, a preadolescent boy, an African-American woman and 42-year-old Jennifer Jason Leigh.

Aviva is determined to have a child, reasoning that by having a baby, she will find the unconditional affection she seeks. Aviva gets pregnant with the awkward assistance of a family friend's teenage son (Robert Agri).

Her "sensible" mom, Joyce (Ellen Barkin), tries to talk her into having an abortion. When persuasion fails, Joyce strong-arms Aviva into undergoing the procedure. The "problem" is thus solved, but with tragically ironic consequences.

Still resolved to get pregnant, Aviva runs away from home, assuming the name she intended for her aborted child, Henrietta. Stowing away on an 18-wheel truck, she naively gives herself to the disreputable driver (Stephen Adly Guirgis), mistaking his lustful predations for genuine affection. Later, he is revealed to be a "pro-life" assassin.

Aviva's travels leads her to Mama Sunshine (Debra Monk), a cheery evangelical who runs a household of variously disabled children, bakes "Jesus tear" cookies and serves "freedom toast" for breakfast.

The prodigal daughter eventually finds her way home (played by the much older Leigh as if to visually convey Aviva's premature loss of innocence) where she discusses the film's other main theme -- free will -- with her nihilistic cousin Mark (Matthew Faber), who is ostracized by his other relatives over rumors of pedophilia.

While Solondz contends that he had no interest in pushing a particular agenda, "Palindromes" remains a politically -- as well as philosophically -- charged film. The issue of abortion and the debate surrounding it haunts practically every frame.

Solondz avoids taking sides, mocking abortion advocates and opponents in equal measure, while managing to make their representative characters somewhat sympathetic.

Joyce epitomizes the hypocrisy of many arguments supporting legal abortion and her hollow-sounding attempt to defend her own earlier abortion -- "I wouldn't be able to afford the treats I get you, the *Nsync tickets and the Gap accounts and we'd be miserable" -- typifies the selfish impulse underscoring such rationalizations. But Joyce, despite her moral myopia, is trying to be a good mother.

Conversely, the film also criticizes pro-lifers who would justify murder to protect the unborn. Still, while Christians are often easy targets for ridicule, Solondz portrays Mama Sunshine as a compassionate, if self-righteous, woman with sincere convictions who loves the discarded children she takes into her home. (Her complicity in a plot to assassinate an abortionist is left uncomfortably ambiguous, however).

In one touching tableau, Aviva sits at breakfast surrounded by Mama Sunshine's born-again flock. Some are missing limbs; others are mentally challenged or blind. It is a rare tender moment and brings into sharp relief Joyce's callous earlier comment about "deformed" babies.

Given Solondz's provocateur leanings, he exhibits surprising sensitivity in his handling of several scenes, including the painful aftermath of the abortion during which Aviva, rejecting her mother's dismissive reassurances that it was "just like a tumor," heart-wrenchingly implores, "Was it a boy or a girl?"

However, the movie's troublesome depictions of what amounts to statutory rape and underage sex, no matter how delicately handled, are as unsettling as they are egregiously unwarranted.

No matter how you look at it -- backward or forward -- the "Palindromes" journey is a cheerless one which many moviegoers may have little interest in taking.

The film contains explicit though nongraphic sexual content, including pedophilia and sex between minors, brief violence and some rough and crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. It was not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
